en: The Chart of the Succession of Masters and Disciples in the Chan Gate of Transmitting the Mind-Ground of China, compiled by the Inner-Chapel Śramaṇa Zongmi, in response to the questions of Prime Minister Pei Xiu.
Prime Minister Pei Xiu asked: [text continues]
The Dharma of Chan has spread widely, yet its followers differ in their lineages, disparaging one another and refusing to harmonize.

It is essential to distinguish their sources and currents, and to understand their respective depths and shallows; although I have devoted attention to this, I have not yet achieved clarity. As I compile these records, I fear there may be errors.
I humbly request that you briefly categorize and differentiate them, providing a general outline of perhaps three or five pages, specifically setting forth the Northern School.
The Southern School. Within the Southern School, there are the schools of Heze, Hongzhou, Niutou, and others.
To fully explain their respective depths and shallows, sudden and gradual approaches, and the essentials of their strengths and weaknesses will serve as a lifelong mirror for me. (Hui) bows twice.
Chan Master Zongmi replied:
"That which was transmitted by Bodhidharma originally has no dual dharmas. Later, it changed according to people, and thus appeared to have divergent paths.

If one locks oneself within [a single perspective], both are non-existent; if one harmonizes them, both are complete. What was previously described in the biographies discussed only one direct lineage."

To discern the lineages of the various masters, one must know that there are both collateral and direct transmissions. For now, I shall first set forth the collateral and direct relationships between teachers and disciples;
thereafter, I will describe the relative depth of their teachings. In this way, it will naturally become clear how the mind of Bodhidharma flowed down to Heze.

As for the Ox-Head School (*Goutou zong*), it branched out from the Fourth Patriarch. Its founder was Master Huìróng, whose spiritual nature was lofty and simple, and whose divine wisdom was keen and sharp.

Having previously spent many years investigating the teachings of the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, he had already realized that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and that deluded emotions are but false attachments.
Later, he met the Fourth Patriarch, who certified his understanding of the principle of emptiness.
However, by manifesting the wondrous nature of non-emptiness within emptiness, one attains awakening and clear understanding without requiring prolonged study.
The Fourth Patriarch said: "This Dharma has, from the beginning, been entrusted to but a single person. I have now finished entrusting it to my disciple Hongren (who is the Fifth Patriarch).
You may establish your own tradition separately. Thereafter, he subsequently established a separate lineage at Mount Niutou.
One school: this was the first patriarch. Through successive transmission it reached the sixth generation (after the fifth patriarch, Zhìwēi, there was a disciple named Mǎsù;
Mǎsù had a disciple named Dàochīn, who is the one from Jìngshān). This school has no connection whatsoever with the Southern and Northern schools.

These two schools—the Southern and Northern—originated specifically from the gate of the Fifth Patriarch. Prior to the Fifth Patriarch, the designations "Southern" and "Northern" did not exist at all.

As for the Northern School, it branched out from the Fifth Patriarch. It is said that there were ten people, including Shenxiu and others, who were all disciples of the Great Master Ren of the Fifth Patriarch.
The Master certified them, declaring each capable of being a teacher in his own region;

therefore, people of the time spoke of "the ten characters born of Ren" (Master Neng directly inherited the legitimate lineage and was not among these ten). Among them were Xiu, the Venerable An, and Zhi.
Xun’s realization of the Way and his virtue were most eminent; both were revered as teachers by Emperor Gaozong.
Their descendants have inherited their legacy, continuing without interruption to this day. Among them, Xiu’s disciple Puji saw his spiritual influence flourish even further;

he served as the Dharma Master of the two capitals and the preceptor at the gates of three emperors. He was known simply as a follower of the Bodhidharma lineage and did not employ the designations of the Northern or Southern schools.

The Southern School refers to the Great Master Huineng of Caoxi; it is the fundamental school that has transmitted the Dharma-garment and the teaching through successive generations since receiving the essential instructions of Bodhidharma.
Later, this was contrasted with Shenxiu, who extensively propagated the gradual teachings in the North.
Therefore, it is called the Southern School. The origins of its transmission are known throughout the world; thus, they shall not be recounted here.

Later, when he wished to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma-seal to Heze, commanding him to carry on the lineage. The origins of this succession have already been presented in a previous account, though it was quite brief.
Now, having received your detailed inquiry, I shall further summarize the ancestral records of the transmission from above.
It is slightly more extensive. In the section of the *Biographies* concerning Master Neng, it states: "There was a monk from Xiangyang named Shenhui, whose secular surname was Gao.
At the age of fourteen (this is Heze; Heze is the name of the monastery where he resided during the transmission of the Dharma), he came to visit the Master.
The Master asked: 'Venerable one, you have come from afar with great hardship. Have you brought your original nature? He replied: 'I have brought it. If there is an original nature, then..."
The Master of Consciousness asked. Shenhui replied, "Awakening takes non-abiding as its foundation; seeing is itself the master.
The Great Master said, "Shasha-mi, how dare you speak so recklessly? He then struck him repeatedly with his staff. Under the blows of the staff, Shenhui reflected:
"A true Great Good Friend is difficult to encounter throughout kalpas. Now that I have met one, how could I begrudge my own life? The Great Master observed this...
He deeply realized that [Huineng’s] feelings were sincere; therefore, he tested him (just as Yao tested Shun by subjecting him to various hardships).

At the end of the biography, it further states that when the Master was about to enter nirvana, he silently received a secret transmission from Shenhui. The words said: "From the beginning of our lineage until now, the authentic succession has been transmitted to only one person.
Internally, the Dharma-seal is transmitted to seal one's own mind; externally, the robe is transmitted to serve as the definitive mark."

This is the essential purpose. However, for the sake of this robe, I have nearly lost my life (referring to the incidents of the Northern School stealing the robe mentioned in the preceding text of this transmission;
it cannot be recorded here). Master Bodhidharma’s prophetic declaration stated: "After the sixth generation, your life will be like a dangling thread"—this refers to you.
Therefore, this robe should remain here to serve as a guardian of the mountain. Your karmic affinity lies in the north.

"You must immediately cross the mountain pass. Twenty years from now, you shall propagate this Dharma and extensively deliver sentient beings. When the Master was nearing death, his disciples Xingtao, Chaosu, Fahai, and others asked, "To whom does the Master’s Dharma legacy belong? The Master replied, "That which has been entrusted to me shall be propagated in the northern lands twenty years hence. They asked again, "Who will it be? He answered: "An old man from the south, With a head like a white ox; He will carry my Dharma robe And transmit my Dharma seal. The disciples then said, "We do not understand these words. The Master said, "I have already explained them to you all. Later, when the monk Huiming arrived, the Master told him, "The one who will receive my Dharma is here. He then called for Huiming to come forward. Upon seeing him, the Master sighed deeply and said, "This is indeed the person. He then presented him with his Dharma robe and Dharma seal, saying, "Twenty years from now, you shall propagate the Dharma in the north. You must protect yourself well. After speaking these words, he passed away. The following year, the Tang dynasty began. Twenty years later, during the Kaiyuan era, Huineng received the transmission of the Dharma in the north. This was precisely as the Master had prophesied. It is said that the Master’s remains were enshrined at Huangmei Mountain. His disciples built a stupa there, and the Emperor bestowed upon it the name "Great Compassion. It is still extant today. The Master’s secular surname was Luo, and his courtesy name was Daoyou. He was born in Shixing County, Hengzhou. His father, Luo Gongyue, served as the Magistrate of Shixing. At age thirty-one, the Master left home and became a monk under Master Daoxin at Dongshan. He studied the path for eight years before receiving the full precepts. He then traveled to Mount Shuangfeng, where he stayed for over thirty years. He never once descended the mountain, nor did he ever speak of worldly affairs. He lived in seclusion, practicing austerities, and attained the Way. He passed away on the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Yongchun era (675). He was seventy-six years old. His secular surname was Lu, and his courtesy name was Zhihui. He was born in the village of Huatai, in the district of Nanhai, Guangzhou. His family was poor, and he supported himself by gathering firewood and selling it. At age twenty-three, he encountered the Fifth Patriarch, who recognized his potential and instructed him to go to Caoqi. There, he labored for fifteen years, serving as a rice-pounder and a woodcutter. One day, while the Fifth Patriarch was walking about, he saw Huineng and said, "There is a person here who can receive the Dharma. He then gave him the Dharma robe and Dharma seal, saying, "Go to the north and propagate the Dharma. Protect yourself well. Huineng then set out for the north. He arrived in Shaozhou and stayed at the Baojing Temple. He lived in seclusion for sixteen years, never revealing his identity. During the Kaiyuan era, he was summoned to the capital and received imperial honors. He passed away on the twenty-fifth day of the first month in the third year of the Tianbao era (764). He was seventy-six years old. His remains were enshrined at Nanhua Temple. The Emperor bestowed upon it the name "Great Wisdom. It is still extant today. The Master’s secular surname was Chen, and his courtesy name was Hongjing. He was born in the village of Xianglin, in the district of Jinyang, Taiyuan. His family was poor, and he supported himself by gathering firewood and selling it. At age twenty-three, he encountered the Fifth Patriarch, who recognized his potential and instructed him to go to Caoqi. He said, "If you wish to know, catch him on Mount Dayu with a net" (tradition says that "Mount" refers to height; Heze’s surname was Gao).
Therefore, it was shown in secret).
The lineage of Heze is entirely the Dharma of Caoxi; it has no separate teaching or principle. It was established in response to the emergence of the Hongzhou school as a side branch.
Therefore, I shall again set forth its doctrinal title and the origins of its transmission, as already explained above.

However, after the passing of Master Neng, the gradual teachings of the Northern School gradually spread widely (as also narrated above), thereby becoming an obstacle to the propagation of the Sudden Gate.

Consequently, the stele inscription recording the transmission at Caoxi had been rubbed away and replaced; thus, for twenty years, the teachings of our school remained submerged and obscure (the Great Master having suffered a hundred... [omitted]).

Various hardships and such matters are all as previously presented in the *Lüzhuan* (Brief Biography); the full account is in the *Běnzhuan* (Main Biography) [to be presented in detail on another day]. At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, Hézé entered Luò and widely propagated this school.
Only then did it become manifest that Xiù’s lineage was collateral and his Dharma-gate was gradual.

Since the two schools were practiced side-by-side, people of the time wished to distinguish their differences; thus, the names "North" and "South" were designated, beginning from this point. Question: Since...
Heze was established as the seventh patriarch. Why were there no eighth, ninth, or tenth?

Since none were subsequently established, what prevents us from relying on the transmission of the robe as evidence and stopping at the sixth? Answer: If we rely on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), names and numbers are fundamentally non-existent;

even "one" does not persist, so how can one speak of "six" or "seven"? Now, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), masters and disciples transmit [the Dharma] in accordance with worldly custom.

The Dharma has its symbolic manifestations. For example, a state establishes seven ancestral temples; burial takes seven months; mourning garments extend through seven generations (the same applies to both Daoism and Buddhism);
the scriptures speak of seven Buddhas; the number of recitations for dhāraṇīs; the colors and materials of the ritual altar; the expedient means of performing rites;
the distance for prostrating to or circumambulating the Buddha; and the limit for inviting monks—all these are restricted to the number seven. Beyond that, they double to fourteen.
From seven times seven down to six, yet not exceeding eight or nine. The ritual for transmission and reception currently practiced accords with worldly conventions to inspire faith;

what cause for doubt could there be? Thus, in the twelfth year of the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong, an imperial edict was issued for the Crown Prince to assemble various Chan masters to definitively establish the fundamental tenets of the Chan school and to investigate the collateral and orthodox lineages of the Dharma transmission. Consequently, there came to be...
An imperial edict was issued, establishing the Great Master Heze as the Seventh Patriarch; an inscription recording this exists within Shenlong Temple.
Furthermore, an eulogy composed by the Emperor for the Seven Generations of Patriarchs is still in circulation today.
The Hongzhou school originated as a collateral branch descending from the Sixth Patriarch.

It refers to a Chan master surnamed Ma and named Daoyi, who was originally a disciple of Master Jin of Jiannan (the lineage source of Jin being Zhi-shen; this [school] was also neither of the Northern or Southern traditions).

Possessing lofty integrity and the ultimate Way, he was a wandering *dhūta* who practiced seated meditation wherever he went. Upon reaching Mount Nanyue, he met Chan Master Rang and discussed the essence of the school.
In both teaching and principle, none could surpass him; only then did they realize that the transmission of the robe and the Dharma at Caoxi was the legitimate lineage.

They subsequently turned their minds toward his guidance and took up residence in Chuzhou and Hongzhou. Whether in the mountains or in the suburbs, they extensively provided offerings and welcomed practitioners of the Way.
Later, at Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou, he widely propagated the essential teachings of Huairang; thus, people of the time called it the Hongzhou School.
Huairang was a collateral branch of the Caoxi lineage (there were approximately one thousand such branches under Caoxi) and was a fellow student of Heze.
However, he focused solely on personal cultivation and did not originally intend to propagate the Dharma. It was due to Master Ma...
He greatly propagated his teachings, thereby establishing the source of this school.

The above is a brief account of the lineages of the various schools; such is the general outline. However, these may be categorized according to their lateral and vertical relationships, as well as their peripheral and central connections.

The intermingling [of these traditions] makes them difficult to remember; therefore, I have now drawn them out as a diagram, hoping that with a single glance they will not be lost from the depths of one’s mind.

This follows immediately after the preceding section, which has already described the various patriarchs and their disciples. Next, I shall distinguish the profundity or shallowness, and the strengths or weaknesses, of the oral teachings transmitted by them. Now, regarding Chan...
The purport of this gate lies in inward illumination; it cannot be fully described by brush nor proclaimed by speech. Although words may fail to reach it, one may still speak with effort;

though the brush cannot reach it, it is simply difficult to set pen to paper. Now, having no choice but to write, I hope you will perceive it within your own mind rather than being hindered by the text.
However, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted only the Dharma of the mind. Thus he said of himself: "My Dharma transmits mind by means of mind; it does not establish written words.
This mind is the pure, original enlightenment of all sentient beings; it is also called Buddha-nature, or sometimes numinous awareness.
When deluded, it gives rise to all afflictions, yet these afflictions do not depart from this mind. When awakened, it gives rise to boundless wondrous functions.
Sublime function likewise does not depart from this mind. Sublime function and afflictions differ in their merit and fault, yet whether one is enlightened or deluded, this mind remains no different.
If you wish to seek the Buddha-way, you must awaken to this mind; therefore, the patriarchs of successive generations have transmitted nothing but this.
However, if there is a harmonious resonance between the stimulus and the response, then even if one lamp transmits to a hundred thousand lamps, each lamp remains no different from the others.
If the capacity of the recipient and the teaching do not accord, then even if a single voice expounds the Dharma, each person understands it according to their own comprehension;

thus, the divergent doctrines of the various schools are the fault of later generations. For now, I shall briefly describe each school before proceeding to judge which is correct and which is erroneous.
The intention of the Northern School is this: sentient beings inherently possess the nature of awakening, just as a mirror possesses the nature of luminosity.

When afflictions shroud it, it is not seen, just as dust and darkness cover a mirror. If one relies on the teacher’s instructions to still and extinguish deluded thoughts, then when those thoughts are exhausted, the mind-nature awakens and there is nothing that is not known.
This is like polishing away the dim dust; when the dust is gone, the substance of the mirror is bright and pure, and there is nothing [it does not reflect].
Because it does not illuminate, the Patriarchal Master Shenxiu presented this verse to the Fifth Patriarch, saying:
The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is a stand for a bright mirror. It must be wiped clean at all times.
"Do not allow any dust to settle upon this.
The commentary states: "This is merely the aspect of the dependent origination of defilement and purity, a gateway for reversing the flow and turning away from habitual tendencies.

Yet, one fails to realize that deluded thoughts are fundamentally empty and that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure. Since awakening has not yet been thoroughly realized, how could cultivation be said to accord with reality? (In Jian-nan, there was also the school of the Jingzhong [Pure Multitude] tenets.)

This is largely the same as that [previous case]. Furthermore, there is Baotang Zong; his understanding seems similar, yet his practice is entirely different. It would be tedious to describe it in detail; we shall discuss each point one by one when we meet in person on another day.

The meaning of Hongzhou is this: the arising of thought, the movement of a念 (nian), the snapping of fingers, the movement of the eyes, and all that is done and enacted—all these are the Buddha-nature.
It is the total manifestation of its function; there is no other function apart from it. Total greed, anger, and delusion; the creation of good and the creation of evil;

the experiencing of pleasure and the experiencing of pain—all these are the Buddha-nature. It is like flour used to make various foods and drinks; every single one is flour. This is the intended meaning.
When one seeks this body—composed of the four great elements, bones, flesh, throat, tongue, teeth, eyes, ears, hands, and feet—one finds that none of these can themselves speak, see, hear, or move.

For instance, at the moment of death, even though the entire body has not yet decayed, the mouth can no longer speak, the eyes cannot see, the ears cannot hear, the feet cannot walk, and the hands cannot act. Therefore, one knows:

That which is capable of speech and movement must be the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Furthermore, if one carefully examines each of the four elements, bones, and flesh, none of them possess the capacity for the afflictions of greed and anger.
Therefore, we know that greed, anger, and the afflictions are all the Buddha-nature.
The essence of the Buddha-nature is not itself any of these various distinctions, yet it is able to produce all manner of differentiated phenomena; its essence is not manifold.
"Suchness" means that this Buddha-nature is neither noble nor ordinary; it is neither cause nor fruit; it is neither good nor evil;
it is without form and without marks; it is without faculties and without abiding; and so on, up to being without Buddhas and without sentient beings.

"That which can produce all varieties" means that this nature is the function inherent in its very essence; therefore, it can manifest as ordinary or noble, as cause or faculty, as good or evil, and it manifests form.
Manifestations can appear as Buddhas, sentient beings, and even as greed, anger, and so forth.

Yet, if one examines their essential nature, they are ultimately neither visible nor verifiable, just as the eye cannot see itself. From the perspective of their functional application, every movement and activity is [the manifestation];
there is no separate dharma that serves as either the subject of realization or the object realized. This is the intended meaning.
According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it is able to universally bring about all realms of rebirth, experiencing suffering and pleasure together with their causes.

Furthermore, the *Buddhaguhya Sūtra* states that in some Buddha-fields, raising an eyebrow, moving the eyes, smiling, blowing, clearing the throat, or even shaking the body—all such acts are Buddha-activities. Once this principle of awakening and understanding is realized, everything...
The primordial nature is spontaneous and natural; therefore, the practice one undertakes ought to accord with this principle.

Thus, one does not give rise to the thought of severing evil, nor does one give rise to the thought of cultivating the Path. The Path is itself the mind; one cannot use the mind to cultivate the mind.
Evil is also the mind; one cannot use the mind to sever the mind. Neither severing nor creating, acting with effortless spontaneity and mastery—this is called liberation.
Liberated persons have no dharma by which they may be constrained and no Buddha to be realized. They are like empty space, neither increasing nor decreasing;
what need is there for supplementation? Why is this? Because apart from the nature of the mind, not a single dharma can be found. Therefore, simply let the mind be as it is.
This is itself cultivation.
The critique states: This is diametrically opposed to the preceding school. In the former, morning and evening distinctions, as well as all movements and actions, are entirely false;
in this [latter], morning and evening distinctions, as well as all movements and actions, are entirely true. I respectfully inquire whether these two are mutually contradictory.

They revile and slander one another. Even at the end of the day, they are unwilling to meet in harmony. Since their views are as divergent as this, how could they refrain from reviling? If they preserve the views of others, they lose their own;
how could they ever be willing to reach a consensus?
The essential meaning of the Oxhead School is that all phenomena are like dreams; fundamentally, there is no reality. Mind and objects are inherently quiescent; they have not become empty only now.
When one is deluded and takes them to be existent, one perceives matters such as prosperity and decline, honor and meanness.

Since these manifestations involve both opposition and conformity, emotions such as attachment and aversion arise. Once these emotions arise, one is bound by various sufferings. To dream and then experience the results within the dream—what else could it be?

What benefit is there in causing harm? This discerning wisdom is likewise like the mind in a dream; even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvana, it would still be like a dream and like an illusion.
Having realized that all things are fundamentally non-existent, it is only right to relinquish the self and forget emotional attachments.

When delusive emotions are severed, the causes of suffering are eliminated, and one is finally able to cross over all calamities and afflictions; this takes the forgetting of emotion as cultivation. The critique states:
previously, it was held that the constant realization of the absolute reality in every thought-moment is awakening, and following the mind as it is cultivation.

Here, however, it is held that the original absence of phenomena is awakening, and delusive emotion is cultivation. Furthermore, regarding the differences in the views of the three preceding schools: the first [school] holds that everything is entirely delusive; the second...
All things are initially real; subsequently, all things are non-existent. If one speaks in terms of practice: first, one subdues the mind and extinguishes delusions;

next, one follows the nature of the emotions; finally, one rests the mind so that it does not arise. (Zongmi) My nature is fond of investigation, and I have personally consulted each [master] to search out their essential meaning as described above.
If one were to ask these words of mine to those students, they would all fail to acknowledge them. When asked, "Does it exist?"...

The answer is "emptiness. To question emptiness is to acknowledge existence. Some say both are negated; others say both are unattainable. Whether it be cultivation or non-cultivation, all cases are of this nature.

The intention behind this is that one constantly fears falling into mere words and is perpetually wary of becoming stuck in what has been attained; therefore, as soon as words are uttered, they are swept away.

For those who have turned their hearts toward the study [of the Way], one then instructs them in meticulous detail, causing them to engage in contemplation for a long time until they become proficient.
Their practices and understandings are thus established. However, each school further possesses various skillful means for refuting external objections and for guiding their followers;
these cannot be recorded in full detail. For now, I shall merely set forth their essential orientations and present their grand outlines.
The school of Heze is especially difficult to describe in words; it is the fundamental intent behind Śākyamuni’s descent into the world and Bodhidharma’s distant journey here.

If one looks back from this toward what preceded it, this school is utterly different from what came before; yet if one encompasses the preceding through this, what preceded it is entirely identical to this.
Therefore, it is difficult to speak of. Now, I shall attempt to express it: all phenomena are like dreams, as all the Sages have unanimously taught; thus, they are false.
Contemplate original quiescence. The sensory realms are originally empty; the mind of empty quiescence possesses a numinous awareness that is never obscured.
This very awareness within empty quiescence is the "mind of empty quiescence" transmitted by the former Bodhidharma. Whether in delusion or awakening, the mind inherently knows itself;

it does not depend on conditions for its arising, nor does it originate from external objects. Even when deluded, afflictions are known to be non-afflictive; when awakened, spiritual transformations manifest.

One also knows [this]. Yet, this knowing is not a supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi*). Nevertheless, the single word "knowing" is the source of all wonders. It is by becoming deluded regarding this knowing that the mark of self (*ātman*) arises;
one calculates "self" and "what belongs to the self," and love and hatred spontaneously emerge. Following the mind of love and hatred, one immediately becomes good or evil.

As the retribution for good and evil, one receives the forms of the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*), revolving through life after life without end. If one encounters a virtuous friend who opens [the way]...

It is shown that one suddenly awakens to the knowledge of emptiness and stillness. This knowledge is itself without thought and without form; who, then, could possess the mark of self or the mark of others?

One realizes that all marks are empty, and the true mind is without thought. When a thought arises, one immediately awakens to it; once awakened, it is immediately gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies solely herein.
Therefore, although one fully cultivates the myriad practices, one takes only non-thought as the fundamental principle. It is simply by attaining this non-thought...

Then, love and hatred will naturally grow thin; compassion and wisdom will naturally increase and become clear; sinful karma will naturally be severed; and meritorious practice will naturally become diligent.
Regarding understanding, one sees that all marks are non-marks; regarding practice, it is called the cultivation of non-cultivation.
When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are immediately cut off. Once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent illumination manifests before one. This is the application.
It is inexhaustible; this is what is called "Buddha.

Above, each school has been briefly described. Now, I shall clarify their relative depth and shall distinguish between their strengths and weaknesses. Yet, the mind permeates all phenomena, and its meanings and flavors are boundless.
While various teachings elaborate upon these truths, the Chan school provides a concise summary. This summary concerns the nature of phenomena as being both unchanging and conforming to conditions.

There are two meanings. Regarding persons, there are two approaches: sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation. When these two meanings are revealed, one knows the ultimate purpose of the entire canon of sutras and śāstras.
When these two gates are opened, one beholds the tracks of all worthies and sages. The profound intent of Bodhidharma truly lies herein. As for "the unchanging following conditions":
since the principle beyond the phenomenal world is difficult to realize through direct exposition, it is now explained by means of a metaphor.

It serves as a balance and mirror to determine the right and wrong of various schools. (One should apply the dharma to follow the metaphors and provide annotations to correspond with the text, hoping that the dharma and the metaphors will each illuminate one another for easy understanding.

However, when first reading, please simply read the metaphors in their entirety; once you have distinguished the fundamental and the derivative, you may then return to compare and analyze the principles using the annotations.)
It is like a single mani jewel (the one spiritual mind), which is solely round, pure, and luminous (empty, quiescent, and cognizant).

It is entirely devoid of all differentiated forms and characteristics (this cognition is fundamentally free from all discrimination, and likewise lacks the distinctions of holy and ordinary, good and evil).

Because its essence is luminous, when it encounters external objects, it can manifest all differentiated forms and characteristics (because its essence is cognizant, when encountering various conditions, it can discriminate between all that is right and wrong, good and bad, and even manage and perform the myriad activities of both the mundane and supramundane worlds). This...

This is the meaning of following conditions (*pratyaya*). The characteristics of color naturally have distinctions; yet the bright pearl never undergoes change (just as folly and wisdom, good and evil, naturally have their own distinctions;
sorrow, joy, love, and hatred naturally arise and cease, while the cognizing mind never interrupts—this is the meaning of immutability).

Nevertheless, although the colors manifested by the pearl may be hundreds or thousands of kinds, let us now take black, which is diametrically opposed to the bright pearl, to serve as an analogy for the contrast between the numinous, knowing vision and darkness.

Although ignorance is diametrically opposed [to wisdom], it is nonetheless of one essence (the dharma and its analogy are fully established). This means that when a pearl manifests as black, its entire substance is completely black, and no light is seen at all.

Likewise, when the spirit-like, cognizant mind is in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is entirely deluded, ignorant, and characterized by craving; thus, the great perfect mirror-wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*)—the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—is not perceived at all.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The characteristics of body and mind, and so forth, are all ignorance. It is like a foolish child or a rustic countryman who, upon seeing it, simply calls it a black bead.

The deluded person sees only what is fixed and regards it as the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). When someone tells them, "This is a bright pearl," they utterly refuse to believe it and instead resent the person who spoke.
This refers to those who act out of deceit. No matter what various principles one may explain, they ultimately refuse to listen or consider them.

Zongmi frequently encounters such individuals. When told, "You now clearly know and see this as the Buddha-mind," they resolutely do not believe it; instead, they say, "These are merely the words used to entice old women. They flatly refuse to examine the truth, claiming only, "I am of dull faculties and truly cannot enter [the Way].

This is the kind of view held by those attached to signs within the *dharmalakṣaṇa* of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the teachings for humans and devas. Even if there were someone willing to believe that this is a bright pearl, it is because they have personally witnessed its...

"Black" also means being enveloped, covered, and obstructed by blackness; one must wait for it to be polished, wiped, and washed away until the darkness is removed, only then can the appearance of clarity manifest, at which point it is called "personally seeing the bright pearl. (The understanding of the Northern School was thus.
Furthermore, there is another class of people who point out and say: "This very darkness is the bright pearl itself. The substance of the bright pearl can never be seen."
If one wishes to recognize it, then black itself is the bright pearl; even blue, yellow, and all other various colors are likewise so.
This causes the ignorant to believe these words, focusing exclusively on the black characteristic, or identifying various characteristics as the bright pearl.
Or, at another time, they may see a black *maṇi* jewel, a *mici-bui* (rice-blown) blue jewel, or a greenish-blue (*bì*) jewel, and even red jewels or amber.
White quartz and other such gems are all called *maṇi*. Or, at another time, when this *maṇi* jewel does not encounter any colors at all, there is only the appearance of luminous purity;
yet one fails to recognize it because one does not see any colors that can be identified.

This is due to the fear of being restricted to the single characteristic of a bright jewel. (The understanding in Hongzhou was like this. As for those called "fools," they are the later students of that school. "Different"...)

When one sees black beads and the like, it means that when the mind engages with the mundane world and discriminates among sensory objects, one perceives thoughts of greed, hatred, attachment, and pride. Amber and quartz represent thoughts such as kindness, compassion, humility, and respect. "When not facing forms" refers to when these thoughts are not directed toward external objects.

There is no conceptualization whatsoever. There is only luminous purity; one clearly knows for oneself that there is no thought. As for those who are narrow-minded and biased, their cognition is merely partial and restricted).

Furthermore, there is a class of people who, upon hearing it said that the various colors within a pearl are all illusory and that its entire substance is completely empty, immediately conclude that this single bright pearl is itself entirely empty.
They then claim that only when there is nothing at all to be attained is one a person of realization. To recognize the existence of even a single dharma is [already an error].
This is not yet understood. It is a failure to awaken to the fact that the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) are entirely empty; this is the "non-empty pearl" (such is the view of Niutou).

Regarding the phrase "hearing the teaching of emptiness and so forth," this refers to the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras that teach emptiness. Regarding the phrase "reckoning this single grain and so forth," it means reckoning that the fundamental awakened nature (*mūlabodhicitta*) is also empty, such that there is nothing to be grasped. Regarding the phrase "grasping at existence and so forth," it refers to hearing the teaching on the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena and being clearly able to know that this is the true mind of fundamental awakening (*mūlabodhicitta*).

Yet, one instead says that one does not understand or know, claiming that the substance of the mind is not empty. As for what is "not empty," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains it as follows: "It is like the emptiness of a jar. This means that because there is no object within the jar, it is called the "emptiness of the jar"; it does not mean [that the jar itself is non-empty].

"There is no jar. To say "there is no" means that within the mind there are no conceptual thoughts of greed, anger, and so forth; this is called the emptiness of the mind. It does not mean the absence of mind itself. To say "no" is merely to eliminate the afflictions within the mind.

Thus we know that Niu-t'ou merely eliminated what is false, but did not yet reveal what is true. (From here below, all serves as an analogy for Ho-tse’s meaning. How is it that one must simply say it is "only pure, bright, perfect, and luminous" before it can be the substance of the jewel?

(This refers to the empty, quiescent awareness. If one speaks only of empty quiescence without revealing awareness, how is this different from empty space? It is also like a round, polished, and pure ceramic ball; though it is round and pure, it lacks the nature of luminosity. How could it be called a *maṇi* jewel? How could it manifest [reflections]?)

[The reflection is like] the Niu-tou school of Hongzhou, which speaks only of "not having a single thing" and does not manifest numinous awareness; it is also like this. As for its black color, and even all other colors such as blue and yellow—

All these are utterly false (the discrimination between good and evil, as well as all movements and activities—such as those recognized in Hongzhou, where every arising thought and mental movement is taken as such). These characteristics are all delusions; thus the Sūtra says: "Whatever has characteristics is entirely false.
One should know that this school takes what is false for the true nature. When one perceives black, black is fundamentally not black;
it is simply its luminosity. Blue is fundamentally not blue; it is simply its luminosity. This applies to red, white, yellow, and all others in the same way.
However, as for that luminosity, when one encounters the various characteristics of forms, one sees in each instance only a brilliant, pure, and perfectly luminous sphere.

Thus, one is no longer deluded regarding the pearl [itself]. All things are empty; only the mind is unchanging. When deluded, one knows it; one knows that the source is not delusion. When thoughts arise, one knows them; one knows that the source is without thought. This extends even to sorrow and joy, anger and pleasure, love and hatred.

One knows each and every thing; one knows that the source is empty and quiescent. Knowing through emptiness and quiescence, one attains immediate clarity regarding the nature of mind and is free from delusion. All of the above is radically distinct from the various schools. Therefore, the initial heading states: "Viewing the former in light of this" (meaning this is radically different from what preceded it).
If one is simply not deluded regarding the jewel, then blackness is already non-black; blackness itself is the bright jewel. This is true for all colors.

Thus, existence and non-existence are sovereign, and clarity and darkness are interfused—what further obstruction could there be? (This accords with those two schools. That "blackness is already non-black" accords with the Niutou school, which asserts that all things are empty.

That "blackness itself is the jewel" and what follows accords with the Hongzhou school, which asserts that all things are Buddha-nature, and that there is no obstruction whatsoever between the ordinary and the sage, or between good and evil. Therefore, the initial heading merely states that this [text] subsumes the preceding ones.)

The preceding section is entirely identical to this point. From here on follows the meaning of the analogy, which once again concludes the three schools according to the fundamental doctrine of Heze (Huineng).
If one recognizes that the bright pearl is the essence capable of manifesting itself, it is forever without change (Heze school).

To say only that "black" is the pearl (Hongzhou school), or to intend to seek the pearl apart from the black (Beizong school), or to claim that both brightness and blackness are non-existent (Niutou school)—all these are cases of not yet having seen the pearl (the general conclusion). Question: According to the *Mahāyāna*...

The sutras, as well as the Chan traditions of all schools from ancient times to the present—including even what Heze taught—concur that the nature of reality is without arising or ceasing, unconditioned and without marks, without sages and without ordinary beings, and without right or wrong; it cannot be realized and cannot be spoken of.
If this is so, why must one necessarily speak of "spiritual awareness" (*lingzhi*)? Answer: These are all...

These negating terms do not reveal the essence of the mind. If one does not point out that which is presently manifest, ever-cognizant, and never obscured as being one's own mind, then what could be called "unconditioned" or "characterized by non-attributes"?

Thus, we know that all teachings merely describe this cognition as being without arising or ceasing, and so forth. Therefore, Heze points to this cognitive awareness within the state of emptiness and the absence of characteristics.

This enables people to recognize it and thus awaken to their own minds; through successive lives and across many worlds, this realization remains forever uninterrupted until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, Heze [Shenhui] gathered together various expressions such as "non-action" (wuwei), "non-abiding" (wuzhu), and even "the ineffable" (buke shuo).
It is simply said that "empty stillness-awareness" encompasses everything. "Empty" means to empty away all characteristics; it is a term used for negation.
"Stillness" alone is the true nature in the sense of being immutable; it is not the same as a mere void or non-existence.

"Awareness" signifies the manifestation of the essence itself; it is not the same as conceptual discrimination. Only this constitutes the fundamental substance of the true mind. Therefore, from the very first arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment...

Up until the attainment of Buddhahood, it is solely quiescence and solely gnosis—unchanging and uninterrupted. However, according to the various stages (*bhūmi*), its names and meanings differ slightly:
In terms of the moment of awakening, it is called "principle and wisdom" (where principle is quiescence and wisdom is gnosis).

In terms of the period of generating the resolve and practicing, it is called "calm abiding and insight" (where calming the conditions of sensory objects accords with quiescence, and contemplating essence and characteristics merges with gnosis). In terms of the spontaneous fulfillment of practice, it is predominantly referred to as "concentration and wisdom."

Through the cause of cessation (*śamatha*), the mind becomes concentrated; concentration is quiescence and immutability. Through the cause of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), wisdom is generated; wisdom is the knowledge of non-discrimination.

When afflictions are entirely exhausted and one's practice is perfected, the moment of attaining Buddhahood is termed *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. *Bodhi* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "awakening," which is to say, knowing. *Nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term...

This is translated as "quiescence" (which is precisely "stillness"). One should know that from the initial arousal of the mind until the ultimate fulfillment of one's intent, there is only quiescence and only knowing.
If one were to follow the two schools [of thought] and merely speak of emptiness, quiescence, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth, then the meaning of *bodhi* would be lacking.
Question: The Hongzhou school also speaks of "numinous awareness" (*lingjue*) and "reflective illumination" (*jianzhao*). How does this differ from "cognition" (*zhi*)? Answer:

If one relies on multiple meanings to manifest a single essence, then all phenomena are but the One Mind. Why then limit it to numinous awareness, reflective illumination, and the like? Now, we shall address the matter according to its essential nature (*kètì*).

This instruction concerns the nature of mind in both the ignorant and the wise, the good and the evil, and even among birds and beasts; it is thus for all. It is clearly and constantly aware, distinguishing it from wood and stone.
However, such terms as "awakened wisdom" (*jñāna*) do not apply universally. That is to say, the deluded do not awaken, and the foolish lack wisdom.

When the mind is in a state of non-determinative neutrality (*avyākṛta*), it is not termed "reflective illumination" and so forth. How could this be the same as the essence of the mind, which is naturally and eternally cognizant?
Therefore, the Master of the *Huayan* Commentary replied to Emperor Shunzong, saying: "The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that is never obscured. He further stated:
"Spontaneously quiescent awareness," and "simultaneously illuminating quiescent awareness. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* itself also distinguishes between "knowing" (*jñāna*) and "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Moreover, although the Hongzhou school speaks of "numinous awakening," this merely indicates that sentient beings possess it, just as [the sūtras] speak of all having Buddha-nature.
This statement is not a definitive indication; were it to indicate [anything], it would merely say "that which can speak," and so forth.

If one were to interrogate this closely, one would say that all are provisional names (*prajñapti*) and that no fixed dharma exists. Furthermore, to discuss Buddhism as a whole, there are two gates: the gate of negation and the gate of manifestation.

When their actual meaning is investigated, there is both wondrous emptiness and wondrous existence. Emptiness is the fundamental mind, while substance and function are fully present. Now, regarding Hongzhou and Niutou...

They take the erasure of traces as the ultimate goal. While they succeed in grasping the intent behind the teaching of "expelling" [delusions] and the meaning of "true emptiness," thereby establishing its essence (*tǐ*), they fail to grasp the intent of the teaching of "manifestation" and thus lack the function (*yòng*) of "wondrous existence. Question:

In the Hongzhou school, the capacity for speech, movement, and so forth is used to manifest the nature of mind (*xìngxīng*). This corresponds precisely to the teaching of manifestation; it is indeed its function. What, then, is lacking?
Answer: The fundamental substance of true mind has two kinds of function: first, the function of its own nature (*svabhāva*); second, the function of responding to conditions (*pratyaya*).
It is like a bronze mirror: the substance of the bronze is the self-nature body; the clarity of the bronze is the self-nature function;

and the reflections manifested by that clarity are the functions responding to conditions. The reflections appear only when facing conditions, and thus they manifest in a thousand variations; the clarity, however, is the self-nature itself.

The nature is eternally luminous. This luminosity is of a single flavor. By analogy, the mind’s eternal quiescence is the essence of self-nature (*svabhāva*), while the mind’s eternal cognizance is the function of self-nature.
These capacities for speech, discrimination, movement, and so forth, are applications that follow conditions (*pratyaya*).

Now, in the teachings of Hongzhou, the indication of these capacities for speech and so on refers only to the application following conditions; it lacks the function of self-nature. Furthermore, this is the teaching of the Exoteric Vehicle (*vyākhyāna-yāna*).
There is manifestation through inference (*anumāna*) and manifestation through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Hongzhou said: "The essence of mind cannot be pointed out;
one only knows that Buddha-nature exists by verifying it through such things as the capacity for speech. This is manifestation through inference. Heze directly stated:
"The essence of mind is that which is capable of knowing; knowing itself is the mind. To manifest the mind by means of knowing is manifestation through direct perception. Hongzhou lacks this.

The two meanings of "unchanging" and "following conditions" have already been explained above. Next, I shall clarify the two gates of "sudden awakening" and "gradual cultivation. Now, regarding the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā), there are neither Buddhas nor sentient beings; how much less could there be the transmission between teacher and disciple? Since it has now been transmitted from Buddha to Buddha through a succession of patriarchs, we know that—based on this— [The text continues: ...it is established that the Dharma is transmitted through the lineage of the patriarchs. This is the meaning of the gate of gradual cultivation. As for the gate of sudden awakening, it refers to the realization that all phenomena are originally non-arising and that the nature of the mind is inherently pure. Although these two gates appear distinct, they are ultimately one and the same, for the essence of awakening is precisely the principle of True Suchness. Thus, while the gate of gradual cultivation involves practicing according to conditions, the gate of sudden awakening realizes that those very conditions are themselves the unchanging nature.

Therefore, one who attains sudden awakening must still rely on gradual cultivation to eliminate residual habits; conversely, one who practices gradual cultivation must realize that the practice itself is the manifestation of sudden awakening. Only by unifying these two gates can one truly enter the Great Vehicle. This is the essential point of the transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Thus, it is said: "The Dharma is not something that can be grasped by the intellect; it is transmitted only through the seal of the mind-to-mind succession. This concludes the explanation of the two gates of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation.

This is the gateway for people to cultivate, realize, and enter [the path]. Since we are discussing people, there are distinctions between delusion and awakening, beginning and end, and ordinary beings and sages.
To awaken from delusion is to suddenly transform the ordinary into the sacred; this is sudden awakening (*tongwu*).

As for sudden awakening, it means that through beginningless delusion and inversion, one has identified these four elements as the body, false thoughts as the mind, and universally claimed them to be the self. If such a person encounters a virtuous friend...

For them, he explained the meaning of the unchanging nature following conditions, as well as the principles of essence and characteristics, substance and function. Suddenly, they awakened to the realization that this numinous awareness was their own true mind;
that the mind is fundamentally empty and quiescent, boundless and signless, which is itself the Dharma-body; and that body and mind are non-dual.

This is the true self; it is not the slightest bit different from that of all Buddhas. Therefore, it is called "sudden" (*dun*). (The following provides an analogy; the commentary follows the text as it proceeds, correlating the metaphor with the Dharma.

Suppose there is a high official (*buddha-nature*) who dreams (*delusion*) that he is in a prison (*the triple world*). His body (*the fundamental consciousness*) is bound by shackles and chains (*craving and attachment*), and he suffers various anxieties and pains (*all karmic retributions*).
He devises a hundred schemes to escape (*inquiring into the Dharma and practicing diligently*), until he encounters someone who calls out to wake him (*a spiritual friend*). Suddenly, he awakens.

Upon awakening (the mind opening through hearing the Dharma), one finally beholds one's own self (the true self of the *dharmakāya*), which has been from the beginning within one's own home (as the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "the house of ultimate emptiness and stillness").

This is peace and bliss (wherein cessation is joy) and sovereignty (the countless merits inherently present within the essence). It is in no way different from that of all the court officials (sharing the same true nature as all Buddhas).
The principle of their unification is as can be understood from the commentary. Based on these analogies and teachings, each point is clearly elucidated:

it is sufficient to distinguish that although the source of body and mind is one in both dreaming and awakening, when their characteristics and functions are examined, the inverted and the correct are vastly different; one cannot, having awakened, again perform the affairs of a dream.

This serves as a metaphor for how the source of the mind is one, yet delusion and awakening are vastly different: the honors received during a dream (the cultivation of positions such as the Great Brahmā Heaven during delusion) cannot compare to the state of awakening.

At that time, he was serving as a county magistrate (this refers to his initial entry into the stage of the Ten Faiths after awakening). He dreamed of obtaining the seven treasures (this refers to his cultivation of immeasurable merit while deluded).

This did not equal even a hundred coins upon waking (this refers to upholding the five precepts and ten wholesome acts at the time of awakening). Because one is false and the other is true, they cannot be compared (the meaning of various teachings stating that giving three thousand or seven treasures is not as good as hearing a single verse of a gāthā is this very point).
Now, in Hongzhou, it is said merely that greed, anger, precepts, and concentration—these single types—are Buddha-nature.
As for "function," it refers to the deficiency in the function of discerning between delusion and awakening, or inversion and correctness.

His intention lies in True Suchness and the nature of the mind, which is always known as the unchanging nature of moisture. Since the mind is free from delusion, it is not ignorance; it is like the wind suddenly ceasing.
After awakening, clinging to objects naturally subsides, like waves gradually ceasing.

As one nurtures the body and mind with concentration and wisdom, they become increasingly free and autonomous, eventually reaching unimpeded spiritual transformations that universally benefit all sentient beings.

This is like the spring sun melting the ice, irrigating and cleansing so as to bring great benefit to all things. Master Chang of Hongzhou once said: "Greed, anger, compassion, and goodness are all Buddha-nature."

What is the distinction? It is like a person who observes only the nature of moisture and perceives no difference between its beginning and end, yet fails to recognize that saving a boat and capsizing a boat differ vastly in merit and fault.
Therefore, while that school is close to the gate of sudden enlightenment, it is not precise regarding the gate of gradual cultivation.
There is error, yet it is entirely suspended. Because the "Ox-head" [school] reaches emptiness, it is half-realized within the gate of sudden enlightenment;
because it forgets emotion, it is without deficiency within the gate of gradual cultivation.

The Northern School consists solely of gradual cultivation and lacks sudden enlightenment (*sudden awakening*) entirely. Because there is no sudden enlightenment, their cultivation is also not authentic.
In contrast, Heze [Shenhui] maintains that one must first achieve sudden enlightenment and then cultivate based upon that enlightenment. Thus, a sutra states:

"If Bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect *bodhi* (the 'awakening'), they take the mind of pure awareness as their practice. By clarifying all discursive thoughts, they perceive the agitation of consciousness" (the 'cultivation'). This...

The principle of sudden enlightenment followed by gradual cultivation is fully contained within the Mahāyāna of the One Treasury (the Tripitaka). The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* constitute its primary tenets.
However, for the sake of various types of practitioners, skillful means have extensively opened diverse gateways to guide and lead each individual accordingly.

When the perfuming that gives rise to the seeds of habituation serves as the superior condition for life after life, then what is taught by all the various schools is likewise the teaching of the Buddhas;
the texts of the various sūtras and śāstras contain this very principle.

Regarding the *Chart of the Succession of Masters and Disciples in the Zen School that Transmits the Mind-ground of China*, the editor-in-chief of the Continued Tripiṭaka, Nakano Tatsu-e, stated on the twelfth day of the twelfth month of the forty-third year of Meiji:
"This book is a rare work not preserved in other collections; I request that it be transcribed."
It was transcribed and included in the *Zokuzōkyō*; Chén promptly complied with the request, permitted the transcription, recorded the facts of the matter, and handed it over.
On an auspicious day in the first month of the forty-fourth year of Meiji.
Chanted throughout the four seas and transmitted through fifty-four generations of lamps,
the śramaṇa Jōshō respectfully records this on the day and month at the quarters of the Abbot of Myōken Seisho, the Great Head Temple of the Nichiren Shū.
